Hemicelluloses got their name because they are often found with cellulose in plant structures. They are heteropolysaccharides
that contain glucose, other sugars, and a variety of linkages. While some contain saccharide backbones with b(1–4)-linkages, they
are unlike cellulose as they much smaller (DP 500–3000), highly branched, amorphous structures that form weak intrachain bonds.
Rather than ﬁbrous, they are soluble and often viscous making them readily fermented by colonic microbes. Their four classes are as
follows: (1) mixed linkage b-glucans, (2) xyloglucans, (3) xylans, and (4) mannans. b-glucans and xyloglucans have glucose back-
bones, so they will be discussed here.
b-Glucans are water-soluble glucose polymers found in cell walls of certain plants. Linear bacterial and algal glucans have b-
(1/3) glycosidic bonds; whereas branched yeast and mushroom glucans have b-(1/3) and -(1/6), or oat and barley glucans
